checks.claim: Key: a brick at rest on a level stone floor gets an upward push equal to its weight, the same as on the mattress (both at rest, so the total upward force equals gravity's pull on each)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'For an object at rest on a horizontal surface, the normal force typically equals the object's weight' (N = mg). On the sunk mattress the brick is also at rest, so the mattress's total upward push must equal the weight too; the extra sinking changes only how far the surface gives, not the size of the push.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'stronger, since stone is harder' is wrong
checks.note: OpenStax: a surface sags 'until the restoring force becomes as large as the weight of the load'; hardness changes the sag, not the final push.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'weaker, since stone does not sink' and 'zero, since stone cannot push' are wrong
checks.note: OpenStax: 'the table actually sags slightly under the load'; 'the sag is slight so we do not notice it'. A zero push would leave the brick unsupported.

checks.claim: Context: stone is squeezed too little to see and pushes back like a very stiff spring; a mattress only sinks further before its push matches the load
checks.note: OpenStax: 'it will exert a restoring force much like a deformed spring (or trampoline or diving board)'; Grokipedia: a 'restorative force from slight deformations in the materials'.

checks.claim: Context: this push from a surface is called the normal force
checks.note: Grokipedia: the part of the contact force acting perpendicular to the interface, directed away from the surface.

checks.claim: Key: an arrow's length in a force diagram shows how strong the force is
checks.note: Grokipedia: arrow length is 'typically drawn proportional to the force's magnitude'. Oak Year 7 'Using force arrows' (https://www.thenational.academy/teachers/programmes/science-secondary-ks3/units/forces/lessons/using-force-arrows) teaches the same at this grade (a force twice the size gets an arrow twice as long). Not every diagram is to scale, but the convention asked about is length = strength.

checks.claim: Stem: each arrow starts at the object and points the way its force acts
checks.note: Grokipedia: the tail sits at the point of application; 'the arrowhead points in the direction of the force's action'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (how fast it moves, how far it will go, how long the force lasts) are wrong
checks.note: A free-body diagram shows forces only; Grokipedia warns against 'confusing velocity with force directions'. Speed, distance and duration are not encoded by arrow length.

checks.claim: Context: a book still on a table gets two equal arrows, gravity down and the table up
checks.note: Grokipedia (Net force): for a book at rest on a table 'the net force is zero because supporting forces balance out'.

checks.claim: Key: pull bigger than friction, vertical forces balanced, so the net force points right and the sled starts moving right and speeds up
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'The direction of the acceleration matches that of the net force'. Oak Year 7 (https://www.thenational.academy/teachers/lessons/balanced-and-unbalanced-forces): the resultant 'acts in the direction of the bigger force'; an object changes speed 'If the forward force is bigger than the backward force'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'moves right at one steady speed' is wrong
checks.note: Steady speed needs zero net force (Grokipedia: zero net force 'maintains constant velocity'). With the pull arrow longer than friction's, the net force is not zero, so the speed keeps rising.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'stays still, since the forces balance' and 'moves right, then slows to a stop' are wrong
checks.note: The horizontal forces are unbalanced (pull > friction), so it neither stays still nor slows while the diagram holds.

checks.claim: Context: it keeps speeding up as long as she pulls harder than friction holds it back
checks.note: A net force in the direction of motion keeps raising the speed.

checks.claim: Key: at steady speed in a straight line the forward force equals friction plus air resistance
checks.note: Grokipedia: zero net force 'maintains constant velocity (either at rest or in uniform motion)'. Oak Year 7 (https://www.thenational.academy/teachers/lessons/balanced-and-unbalanced-forces): with balanced forces the car 'could be moving forwards at steady speed'.

checks.claim: Stem simplification: 'a forward force from its engine drives it'
checks.note: Strictly the forward push on the car comes from the road on the driven tyres, powered by the engine; school texts call it the engine's driving force. An acceptable grade-level simplification.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'a little bigger', 'much bigger', 'a little smaller' are wrong
checks.note: Any imbalance changes the speed (Oak: 'When forces are balanced there is no resultant force and no change in speed'). Oak lists the misconception that the force's direction shows the direction of motion.

checks.claim: Context: bigger forward force speeds it up, smaller slows it; balanced does not mean still
checks.note: Oak: a car with a bigger backward force 'keeps moving forwards but slows down'; with balanced forces it could be still or moving at steady speed.

checks.claim: Key: when the canopy opens the net force points up, and she keeps falling but more slowly
checks.note: Illinois Q&A: the total force 'right after the parachute opens is upwards'; 'This does not mean he will move in the upwards direction'. Physicslens: the parachutist is 'still moving downward' the whole time.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'She rises upward for a short while' is wrong (not partly true)
checks.note: She never rises relative to the ground; the apparent rise in films is only relative to a camera-flyer still in free fall (Physicslens; Oak Year 8 parachute lesson). Not defensible as right.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'hangs still in the air for a while' and 'keeps falling at the same speed' are wrong
checks.note: Her downward speed drops sharply but stays above zero; it does not stay the same because the net force is no longer zero.

checks.claim: Context: 'An unbalanced force against an object's motion slows it without turning it around'
checks.note: False as a general rule: a ball thrown straight up has gravity, an unbalanced force against its motion, and gravity slows it AND turns it around. What keeps the skydiver from turning around is that the air's push weakens as she slows and matches gravity again while she is still moving down (Illinois Q&A: 'As the parachute slows down, the upward air friction force drops'). Fix: 'The net force now points up, against her motion, so it slows her fall. It cannot send her up: as she slows, the air's push weakens until it matches gravity again, while she is still moving down, and she drifts down at a gentle steady speed of about 5 to 8 metres a second.'

checks.claim: Context: open-canopy steady speed about 5 to 8 metres a second
checks.note: Grokipedia: the canopy lowers terminal velocity 'to 5-8 m/s (11-18 mph)' (its intro says 5-7 m/s). Skydiving sources found by search put a modern canopy near 1,000 ft per minute (about 5 m/s), faster canopies up to about 7.6 m/s and big student canopies slower, so 'about 5 to 8' holds as a typical range.

checks.claim: Context: films seem to show her shooting up because the camera-flyer is still falling fast
checks.note: Oak Year 8: 'Video of skydiving may lead pupils to think opening a parachute makes a skydiver shoot upwards', explained as motion relative to the cameraman; Physicslens: 'The camera-holder is still dropping rapidly, but the parachutist has slowed down'.

checks.claim: Key: place the magnet beside the path on the cup's side, so its pull bends the ball's path toward the cup
checks.note: PBS Design Squad 'Invisible Force' (leader notes https://dcmp.org/guides/TID9868_2.pdf): the challenge is a setup where a steel ball rolling past a magnet changes direction and hits a target off to the side; the ball is pulled toward the magnet. A magnet attracts iron and steel (Grokipedia Magnet: 'Ferromagnetic materials show strong attraction to magnetic fields').

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Beside the path, opposite the cup' is wrong
checks.note: Unmagnetised steel is attracted, not repelled, so a magnet on the far side pulls the ball away from the cup.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'In the path, just ahead of the ball' and 'Above the path, over the ball' are wrong
checks.note: Ahead of the ball the pull is along the path (the ball runs straight at the magnet); above it the pull is upward. Neither gives the sideways pull needed to swerve toward a cup off to one side.

checks.claim: Context: a magnet pulls steel across a gap without touching; a sideways unbalanced force bends the path; a push must come from the far side
checks.note: Grokipedia: magnetic forces act 'without the need for physical touch'; a push toward the cup is applied from the side opposite the cup.

checks.claim: Key: the air pushes back harder as she speeds up, until it matches her forward push and her speed holds steady
checks.note: Science Learning Hub: 'As you go faster, the force of air resistance pushing back on you increases'; 'Eventually, the forces become balanced'; 'Once the forces become balanced, your speed stays the same'. Grokipedia Drag: 'a cyclist experiences significant air drag that increases with speed'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Gravity pulls back harder as she speeds up' is wrong
checks.note: On flat ground gravity pulls toward Earth's centre (straight down) and does not change with speed.

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'A steady push can give only a steady speed' and 'Her bike can store only so much force' are wrong
checks.note: Science Learning Hub: the forward force speeds the cyclist up 'until the drag becomes the same size as the forward force'; 'Speed will always change until forces become balanced again'. A force is not stored in a bike (Oak lists 'An object has force' as a misconception).

checks.claim: Context: once air's push matches her forward push the forces balance; gravity on flat ground pulls down, not back
checks.note: Simplified (rolling resistance also acts, roughly constant with speed), but the growing force that sets the top speed is air resistance, as the key says.

checks.claim: Key: contact vs non-contact is decided by whether the objects must touch
checks.note: Grokipedia: a contact force 'arises from the direct physical interaction between two objects touching each other'; non-contact forces 'act through fields or media without the need for physical touch'. Oak Year 7: 'Contact forces only act when objects are touching'; 'Non-contact forces can act with or without the objects touching' (https://www.thenational.academy/teachers/programmes/science-secondary-ks3/units/forces/lessons/the-different-kinds-of-force).

checks.claim: Grouping: gravity and magnetism non-contact; friction and the normal force contact
checks.note: Grokipedia lists frictional and normal forces as contact forces and gravitational and magnetic forces as non-contact; Oak's exit quiz marks magnetic force and weight non-contact, friction contact.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (needs air, works only on metals, strong or weak) are wrong
checks.note: Gravity needing air is a documented misconception; gravity acts on all matter (Grokipedia Gravity: between any two objects with mass); friction and normal forces act on non-metals too; strength does not define the groups.

checks.claim: Context: Earth pulls a falling apple and a magnet pulls a paper clip before anything touches; gravity needs no air and pulls on everything
checks.note: Plain example, not the Newton apple story. A steel paper clip is ferromagnetic and attracted across a gap.

unit_notes: One error, in context only: question 307ddce173 states as a general rule that an unbalanced force against an object's motion slows it 'without turning it around', which is false (gravity turns a ball thrown upward around). The key and all choices of that question are sound; the fix rewords the context to say the air's push weakens as she slows. Horizon Research's ATLAST manual (cited in facts.md) could not be read as text by the fetch tool, so its quotes were not relied on; Oak, Grokipedia, OpenStax, the Science Learning Hub and the Illinois Q&A covered every claim instead.
